competitions.name: Modded-NanoGPT Speedrun
competitions.tagline: Train a GPT-2-level LM to a target FineWeb val loss as fast as possible on 8xH100.
competitions.description: The NanoGPT speedrun is a competitive benchmark where contributors search for the fastest training algorithm that reaches a fixed cross-entropy loss on the FineWeb validation set using 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Track 1 targets 3.28 loss (GPT-2 Small level), Track 2 targets 2.92 loss (GPT-2 Medium level), and Track 3 minimizes step count under a fixed architecture/data/batch-size with unlimited wallclock. Records are submitted via pull requests, validated by re-running on the same hardware, and require statistical significance (p<0.01) over multiple runs. The benchmark is run by Keller Jordan and a large community of contributors.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a PR to master adding a record folder under records/track_1_short/ (or track_2_medium/, track_3_optimization/) with the modified train_gpt.py and run logs demonstrating the new record.
participation.submissionFormat: Modified train_gpt.py plus run logs (multiple seeds) showing mean val loss and timing; PR description with the claimed record.
participation.computeDetails: Official records are timed on 8x NVIDIA H100 GPUs (sponsored by PrimeIntellect). Track 3 allows unlimited wallclock budget.
participation.eligibility: Open to anyone; records must be reproducible on the same hardware.
participation.verification: Re-run on the same hardware; submissions must provide enough run logs to reach p<0.01 statistical significance that mean val loss meets the target.

competitions.quickstart:
git clone https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt.git && cd modded-nanogpt
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install torch==2.10 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
python data/cached_fineweb10B.py 9
./run.sh

competitions.name: AssetOpsBench
competitions.tagline: Build and evaluate industrial AI agents that turn operational evidence into reliable maintenance actions.
competitions.description: AssetOpsBench is an open ecosystem and benchmark for industrial AI agents, connecting sensor observations, failure knowledge, time-series analysis, and maintenance workflows through MCP servers. The research benchmark includes 141 expert-curated scenarios (99 single-agent, 42 multi-agent), scored by trajectory-based evaluation with LLM-as-Judge and static JSON scorers. It is maintained by IBM Research and has spawned public competitions (CODS 2025, IJCAI 2026) and a family of related benchmarks.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a Pull Request or an Issue tagged `new-scenario` to contribute scenarios; competition submissions go through Codabench (CODS) or Kaggle (IJCAI).
participation.submissionFormat: Scenario definitions following the Utterance and Ground Truth design guidelines; agent trajectories evaluated via `uv run evaluate`.
participation.computeDetails: MCP servers and CouchDB run locally; agent runs require LLM API access (TokenRouter / LiteLLM proxy).
participation.eligibility: Open to researchers, engineers, educators, students, and domain experts.
participation.verification: Trajectory-based offline evaluation with LLM-as-Judge and static_json scorers; competition tracks use public and hidden evaluation.

competitions.quickstart:
git clone https://github.com/IBM/AssetOpsBench.git
cd AssetOpsBench
pip install -e .
uv sync
cp .env.public .env
uv run evaluate --trajectories traces/trajectories --scenarios /path/to/scenarios_data --scorer-default static_json --reports-dir reports/static_json_eval

problems.description: Agents must coordinate MCP tools and operational evidence to complete industrial operations tasks across 141 expert-curated scenarios (99 single-agent, 42 multi-agent). Scored by trajectory-based evaluation against expert-defined ground truth.
problems.name: Industrial Asset Operations Agent Scenarios

competitions.name: AlpacaEval
competitions.tagline: Maximize LLM win rate against a reference model as judged by an automatic annotator.
competitions.description: AlpacaEval is an automatic evaluator for instruction-following LLMs: a model's outputs on the 805-example AlpacaEval set are compared pairwise against a reference model (text-davinci-003 for AlpacaEval 1.0, gpt4_turbo for AlpacaEval 2.0) and an LLM annotator picks the preferred output. The win rate is the fraction of instructions where the model beats the reference; AlpacaEval 2.0 additionally reports a length-controlled win rate from a logistic regression that debiases output length. Maintained by the tatsu-lab group (Stanford), it is designed as a fast (<5 min), cheap (<$10) proxy for human preference that correlates 0.98 with ChatBot Arena.

participation.howToSubmit: Fork the repo, add a model config under src/alpaca_eval/models_configs/<model_name>, run `alpaca_eval evaluate_from_model --model_configs '<model_name>'`, then open a PR adding the config, the outputs json, the annotations, and the updated leaderboard CSV under src/alpaca_eval/leaderboards/.
participation.submissionFormat: Model config YAML, model_outputs.json (instruction/output per example), annotations.json, and an updated leaderboard CSV entry.
participation.computeDetails: Evaluation itself is API-based (no GPU). A GPU is only needed if you decode from a local HuggingFace model; API models need none.
participation.eligibility: Open to anyone; top-5 models can request verification by a core maintainer.
participation.cost: free (you pay your own annotator API costs, <$10 per run)
participation.verification: Community submissions are self-reported; core maintainers re-run decoding and evaluation for top-5 models to mark them 'verified'.
requirements: GPU only for local HuggingFace models

competitions.quickstart:
pip install alpaca-eval
export OPENAI_API_KEY=<your_api_key>
alpaca_eval --model_outputs 'example/outputs.json' --annotators_config 'weighted_alpaca_eval_gpt4_turbo'
# or, to also generate outputs from a HF/API model:
alpaca_eval evaluate_from_model --model_configs 'oasst_pythia_12b' --annotators_config 'alpaca_eval_gpt4_turbo_fn'

problems.description: Length-controlled win rate of a model's outputs over the gpt4_turbo baseline on the 805-example AlpacaEval set, judged by the weighted_alpaca_eval_gpt4_turbo annotator. The length-controlled metric fits a logistic regression on output length difference to debias the raw win rate.

competitions.name: CogDL Graph Learning Leaderboards
competitions.tagline: Benchmark and compare graph deep learning methods on standard node, link and graph classification datasets.
competitions.description: CogDL is a graph deep learning library from Tsinghua's THUDM that maintains public leaderboards of state-of-the-art results for unsupervised and semi-supervised node classification, multiplex node classification, link prediction, multiplex link prediction, knowledge graph completion and graph classification. Methods are implemented in the toolkit and their accuracy / F1 / ROC-AUC / MRR values across standard datasets are tabulated in results.md. New models are contributed by opening an issue and submitting a pull request that implements the model and passes the unit tests, after which results are added to the leaderboards.

participation.howToSubmit: Open an issue describing your algorithm, then submit a pull request implementing the model in cogdl/models with a corresponding unit test; accepted results are added to the leaderboards in results.md.
participation.submissionFormat: Model implementation under cogdl/models (plus an example script under examples/) and a unit test in tests/tasks/ following the existing format.
participation.computeDetails: Most GNN benchmarks run on a single GPU; multi-GPU parallel runs are supported via --devices.
participation.verification: Travis CI runs the unit tests and enforces code coverage on the pull request before results are added.

organizer.name: CogDL Team (Tsinghua University, ZJU, DAMO Academy, ZHIPU.AI)

competitions.quickstart:
pip install cogdl

# run GCN and GAT on Cora over 5 seeds
python scripts/train.py --dataset cora --model gcn gat --seed 0 1 2 3 4

competitions.name: MLE-bench
competitions.tagline: Maximize Kaggle medal rate across 75 ML engineering competitions by building autonomous ML agents.
competitions.description: MLE-bench evaluates AI agents on 75 Kaggle competitions, measuring the percentage of competitions where the agent's submission earns a medal (Any Medal %). Agents are given 24 hours and a standard compute budget (36 vCPUs, 440GB RAM, 1x24GB A10 GPU) to produce CSV submissions that are graded against held-out test splits. The benchmark is maintained by OpenAI and submissions are made via pull requests adding grading reports to the runs/ directory. It matters because it measures end-to-end ML engineering capability of autonomous agents.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a PR to main adding grading reports under runs/<run-group>/ and updating runs/run_group_experiments.csv with an experiment id, then update the README leaderboard table.
participation.submissionFormat: Grading report JSON files organized in runs/ by run group, plus a row in the README leaderboard table with mean ± SEM of any_medal_percentage across splits.
participation.computeDetails: Recommended: 36 vCPUs, 440GB RAM, 1x24GB A10 GPU, 24 hours runtime. Lite split can run on less.
participation.rounds: Continuous; submissions accepted via PR (currently paused as of 2026-04-24 while a new fairness process is developed)
participation.eligibility: Open to all; agents/teams submit results via PR
participation.verification: Human review of PR + grading reports; rule violation and plagiarism detectors available in extras/

competitions.quickstart:
pip install -e .
mlebench prepare --lite
mlebench grade-sample <PATH_TO_SUBMISSION> spaceship-titanic
uv run python experiments/aggregate_grading_reports.py --experiment-id <exp_id> --split low

competitions.name: CyberGym
competitions.tagline: Evaluate AI agents on real-world vulnerability analysis: generate a PoC that crashes the vulnerable build but not the patched one.
competitions.description: CyberGym is a large-scale cybersecurity benchmark built from real-world OSS-Fuzz and ARVO vulnerabilities. An agent receives a pre-patch (vulnerable) program and must produce a proof-of-concept input that triggers the vulnerability; the submission server verifies it against both the vulnerable and patched builds. Submissions to the leaderboard are made by email or GitHub issue with a structured report covering success rate and cost, and the organizers maintain the benchmark and leaderboard.

participation.howToSubmit: Email a structured report to zhun.wang@berkeley.edu or open a GitHub issue with your results and artifacts, including an icon for your system.
participation.submissionFormat: Structured report with fields: agent_name, success_rate, link, category, models[] (name, input_tokens, ...), plus cost reporting and a public writeup/paper/blog link.
participation.computeDetails: Server data is large (~10TB full, ~130GB binary-only); agent compute depends on the submitted system.
participation.eligibility: Open to all; submissions must report cost alongside success rate.
participation.verification: PoCs are verified by the submission server against vulnerable and patched builds; reported costs are estimates and reviewed by organizers.

competitions.quickstart:
pip3 install -e '.[dev,server]'
git lfs install
git clone https://huggingface.co/datasets/sunblaze-ucb/cybergym cybergym_data
python3 -m cybergym.server --host $HOST --port 8666 --mask_map_path mask_map.json --log_dir ./server_poc --db_path ./server_poc/poc.db
python3 -m cybergym.task.gen_task --task-id arvo:10400 --out-dir ./cybergym_tmp --data-dir ./cybergym_data/data --server "http://$HOST:8666" --mask-map mask_map.json --difficulty level1
bash ./cybergym_tmp/submit.sh ./cybergym_tmp/poc

problems.description: Fraction of vulnerability analysis tasks solved by an agent, with cost reported alongside success rate.
problems.name: CyberGym Leaderboard

competitions.name: ClawProBench
competitions.tagline: Evaluate AI models inside the live OpenClaw runtime on 102 agent scenarios, ranked by FinalScore.
competitions.description: ClawProBench is a live-first benchmark harness that runs AI models as agents inside the OpenClaw runtime across 102 active scenarios (164 catalog) spanning six domains, graded deterministically by scenario-specific checkers. Models are ranked by FinalScore = 100 × S^0.40 × r_all^0.45 × r_any^0.15, where S is average_score, r_all derives from pass^3 and r_any from pass@3, weighting stable repeated success most heavily. It is maintained by YuanHang Xiao (suyoumo) with a public leaderboard, an arXiv paper, and a Hugging Face dataset release; results are published by the organizers, who also invite third-party API providers to submit models for reproducible evaluation.

participation.howToSubmit: Run the harness locally against a model and contact the organizers (xyh920691910@outlook.com) to submit results or discuss evaluation for the leaderboard; third-party API gateway providers can request that their served models be benchmarked and published.
participation.submissionFormat: Benchmark reports written to results/ by run.py, containing per-scenario scores, pass^3, pass@3, average_score, FinalScore, cost, latency and resume metadata.
participation.computeDetails: Runs against a live local OpenClaw runtime; model inference is via the provider's API, so compute depends on the model endpoint used.
participation.rounds: Continuous leaderboard updates; multi-trial runs via --trials N (default 3)
participation.eligibility: Open to model providers and third-party API gateway providers; organizers run and publish reproducible results when the evaluation setup is stable.
participation.verification: Deterministic scenario-specific graders and custom checkers in custom_checks/, with trace-aware scoring and regression tests in tests/.

competitions.quickstart:
pip install uv
uv venv --python 3.11
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -r requirements.txt
openclaw --help
python3 run.py inventory
python3 run.py run --model '<MODEL>' --execution-mode live --benchmark-profile core --trials 1 --cleanup-agents

competitions.name: Polymarket Paper Trader — Forecast Arena & AI Trader Leaderboard
competitions.tagline: Forecast real Polymarket questions or paper-trade them; scored by Brier score and ROI against the crowd.
competitions.description: A zero-risk gym and benchmark for AI agents on real Polymarket prediction markets. The Forecast Arena has AI models and naive baselines publish one YES probability per soon-resolving market before it resolves, scored by Brier score, calibration error and alpha vs the crowd. A separate AI Trader Leaderboard ranks agents by ROI% on a $10k paper account with real order books and official fees. Run by the agent-next community; the point is measuring decision intelligence against real market outcomes.

participation.howToSubmit: Forecast Arena: add your entrant to benchmark/arena.yaml (id, label, kind, model) and open a PR; the arena workflow runs daily. Trader leaderboard: generate a leaderboard_entry (MCP) or run `pm-trader leaderboard`, then open an issue titled `[SUBMIT] {agent_name} — ROI: {roi}%` with the JSON output.
participation.submissionFormat: arena.yaml entrant entry (litellm model id + disclosure metadata) for the Arena; JSON leaderboard_entry output pasted into a GitHub issue for the trader leaderboard.
participation.computeDetails: Forecasting is a single-shot LLM call per market; no GPU needed. Paper trading hits live Polymarket public APIs.
participation.rounds: Daily forecast rounds; markets selected each run (ending in 0-14 days).
participation.eligibility: Open to any model provider or agent author; entrants with fewer than 20 scored forecasts are listed unranked.
participation.verification: Forecasts are recorded before resolution and scored against real outcomes; append-only JSONL data on the arena-data branch, built by CI. Trader leaderboard entries are self-reported via issue and reviewed.
requirements: API key for your model provider

competitions.quickstart:
pip install -e "benchmark[dev]"
polymarket-benchmark run --model claude-opus-4 --market-set mini

# Forecast Arena local run
polymarket-benchmark arena predict --data /tmp/arena-data
polymarket-benchmark arena resolve --data /tmp/arena-data
polymarket-benchmark arena build --data /tmp/arena-data --out site/

problems.description: AI entrants and naive baselines each publish one YES probability per soon-resolving Polymarket binary market before it resolves; scored by Brier score, calibration error and alpha vs the crowd once outcomes land.
problems.name: Forecast Arena

problems.description: AI agents trade Polymarket with a fixed $10,000 paper balance against live order books and official fees; ranked by ROI% with Sharpe ratio as tiebreaker.
problems.name: Paper Trading Leaderboard

competitions.name: Noise: Speedrun for pretraining without backpropagation
competitions.tagline: Train a fixed 37.7M transformer on 30M FineWeb tokens using only forward passes, minimizing validation loss or time-to-target.
competitions.description: Noise is a pretraining speedrun where the learning algorithm may never run a backward pass: all credit assignment must come from forward evaluations of the model. The model, data (30M-token FineWeb set) and score (mean next-token cross-entropy on a fixed validation set) are fixed; only the learning algorithm changes, and track 3 also frees the architecture. Runs are on one 8xH100 node with seed 0, and records are submitted as PRs that modify the track's training script in place along with the run logs.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a PR that changes the track's training script in place (train/val/run.py, train/speedrun/run.py or train/arch/run.py, plus train/arch/model.py on track 3) and adds the run's logs (config.json, metrics.jsonl, result.json) to the log/ folder next to it.
participation.submissionFormat: Modified training script plus run logs: config.json, metrics.jsonl and result.json from logs/
participation.computeDetails: Official records run on one 8xH100 node; some entries used 8xH200 or 2x RTX 5090.
participation.verification: PR review; a record must beat the current one in its track under the no-backprop rules, judged by the spirit of the rule; logs are included with the script.

competitions.quickstart:
uv sync
uv run utils/prepare_data.py
uv run torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=8 train/val/run.py
uv run utils/eval.py logs/val/final.pt

competitions.name: Skoltech Anomaly Benchmark (SKAB)
competitions.tagline: Detect outliers and changepoints in multivariate industrial sensor time series, scored by F1 and NAB.
competitions.description: SKAB is a benchmark of 34+ multivariate time-series datasets collected from a physical water-pump testbed, with two markups: single-point outliers and collective changepoints. Algorithms are evaluated as binary classification (F1, FAR, MAR) for outlier detection and with the NAB score plus missed-changepoint and false-positive counts for changepoint detection. It is maintained by researchers at Skoltech and targets the anomaly-detection core used in industrial monitoring.

participation.howToSubmit: Present and evaluate your algorithm on the SKAB Kaggle competition page; results are also tracked on Papers with Code.
participation.submissionFormat: Anomaly scores or binary labels per dataset, evaluated with the TSAD evaluation modules.
participation.verification: Evaluation via the TSAD framework on the held-out test set

organizer.name: Skoltech (Iurii D. Katser, Vyacheslav O. Kozitsin)

problems.name: Outlier Detection

competitions.name: JevBench
competitions.tagline: Benchmark for AI decision models measuring typed decision accuracy, calibration, latency and cost.
competitions.description: JevBench by Benchmark Heaven evaluates AI decision models and Jev-compatible systems on typed decisions: given a state, rubric and exact label set, a model returns one typed answer plus a probability distribution. Systems are scored on Intelligence (chance-corrected accuracy), Calibration, Speed and Cost, combined into a JevBench Score. Maintained by Benchmark Heaven independently of TypeSafe AI; the canonical board is at benchmarkheaven.com/jev-models.

participation.howToSubmit: Open an issue or PR with a public endpoint or weights; the maintainers run the frozen decision set through the author's own interface and publish the row.
participation.submissionFormat: A reachable endpoint implementing the author's published interface (TypeSafe-compatible /v1/systemone, list-shaped /decide, Gradio Space, or open weights), plus a documented mapping and cost basis.
participation.computeDetails: Entrants run on the submitter's own hardware or endpoint; the harness itself needs only the standard library for HTTP adapters.
participation.verification: Maintainers run the frozen, hashed decision set serially through the entrant's own interface; mappings and cost bases are pre-registered before runs.

competitions.quickstart:
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v

python -m jevbench.cli run --tasks datasets/public/original.jsonl \
  --adapter typesafe --model jev-latest --key-env TYPESAFE_API_KEY \
  --price-in-per-m 0.042 --price-out-per-m 0 \
  --results RUN/results.jsonl --raw-dir RUN/raw \
  --ledger RUN/ledger.jsonl --cap-usd 15 --manifest RUN/manifest.json

competitions.name: RL-pricing
competitions.tagline: Can deep RL beat 1/N? Submit a long-only portfolio policy and get scored on a causal, live-forward-tested leaderboard.
competitions.description: RL-pricing is a reproducibility lab and benchmark for trading AI. Submissions are long-only portfolio policies that map price history to target weights, filled at the next open with proportional fees, and scored on Sharpe, CAGR, max drawdown, turnover and alpha against 1/N buy-and-hold across fixed historical tasks (crypto majors, US multi-asset, US sectors) plus a live track and a daily decision ledger. It is run by Bicheng Wang and Xinyi Zhang; the point is to test whether published trading-AI claims survive an honest, pre-registered protocol.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a pull request adding only submissions/<id>/ (policy.py + submission.json); CI writes every record under leaderboard/ and rejects PRs that edit them.
participation.submissionFormat: submissions/<id>/policy.py implementing the Policy interface (act, optional fit/save/load) plus submission.json with name, kind, policy reference, trials, authors, description.
participation.computeDetails: PPO takes one to two minutes per seed on a laptop CPU; no GPU required.
participation.rounds: Historical track (fixed windows) plus a live track scored monthly on sessions after a policy's public freeze.
participation.verification: CI checks the submission builds, has no lookahead (rl-pricing bench check-causal), and that baselines reproduce; live policies are frozen with SHA-256 hashes and scored only on sessions after the freeze stamp.

competitions.quickstart:
git clone https://github.com/BichengWang/RL-pricing.git
cd RL-pricing
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e .
rl-pricing bench tasks
rl-pricing bench run --task synthetic --submission momentum --out-root /tmp/board
rl-pricing bench leaderboard --out-root /tmp/board --no-readme

competitions.name: A sharper exponent for integer multiplication
competitions.tagline: Improve the conditional exponent saving κ in T(n)=O(n(log n)^{1-κ}) for integer multiplication.
competitions.description: A community research competition to sharpen the conditional exponent κ in the integer-multiplication bound T(n)=O(n(log n)^{1-κ}), building on OpenAI's September 2026 preprint. Contributors submit PRs with constructions, proofs and finite replays; the maintainer reviews each and records the best reviewed κ as the selected result. It matters because it tracks progress toward sub-n(log n) multiplication, though all results remain conditional on five retained framework assumptions.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a PR to main adding a research package (PROOF.md, certificate, replay scripts) under a new directory; coordinate claims on the discussion board and check handoffs before starting.
participation.submissionFormat: A PR containing a construction/proof package with an exact certificate (JSON), a written proof, and a reproducible verification target (make target or script).
participation.computeDetails: Finite replays and arithmetic checks run on CPU; some Lean formalization packages use pinned toolchains. No GPU required.
participation.eligibility: Open to anyone; agents and donated inference explicitly welcomed.
participation.verification: Maintainer review plus finite replay scripts and Lean kernel checks; results are conditional, not formally verified end-to-end.

links.label: OpenAI preprint: Integer multiplication below n log n

competitions.name: LoRA Speedrun
competitions.tagline: Fine-tune a small LLM to a fixed accuracy target on one L40S in the least training wall-clock time.
competitions.description: A frozen-task speedrun for LoRA fine-tuning: train Qwen2.5-1.5B to ≥57.0% GSM8K exact-match (Track 1) or SmolLM2-1.7B to ≥75.5% SQuAD v1.1 EM (Track 2) on a single Modal L40S, minimizing training wall-clock. Submissions are PRs containing train.py, config.yaml and NOTES.md; a maintainer re-runs each 3× with fresh seeds in a network-blocked sandbox and the mean time becomes the record. It exists to make fine-tuning speedup claims falsifiable, in the spirit of modded-nanogpt.

participation.howToSubmit: Copy submissions/TEMPLATE/ to submissions/NNN-<your-github-handle>/, add train.py, config.yaml and NOTES.md, self-verify with harness/modal_verify.py --runs 3, then open a PR; a maintainer comments /verify to re-run it 3× on spec hardware.
participation.submissionFormat: A directory with train.py (implements --data-dir/--output-dir/--seed), config.yaml (author, technique, hyperparameters, extra pinned pip packages, track), and NOTES.md explaining the mechanism; no adapter weights committed.
participation.computeDetails: Official timing on 1× NVIDIA L40S (48 GB) in a network-blocked Modal sandbox; free via Modal monthly credits. Local iteration on any 24 GB+ card is allowed but not official.
participation.eligibility: Anyone; fork PRs welcome, first outside records already merged.
participation.verification: CI static validation, an advisory Claude security screen, human code review, then 3 fresh-seed timed reruns in a network-blocked Modal sandbox with adapter param-count and content-hash integrity audits.

competitions.description: NavGPT-3 is a hierarchical navigation runtime that combines a Planner (Claude Opus 5 or GPT-6 Astra) with a NavGPT VLA action policy. competitions.name: Mathematics Distillation Challenge — Equational Theories — Stage 2
competitions.tagline: Decide whether one magma law implies another and back every answer with a machine-checked Lean 4 certificate.
competitions.description: Given two equational laws over magmas, decide whether the first implies the second and submit a Lean 4 certificate: a proof for true implications or a magma countermodel for false ones. A deterministic Lean judge accepts or rejects each answer with no partial credit. The competition runs two tracks — Solo (one subprocess per problem, 3600 s each) and Marathon (N problems per subprocess under a shared global budget) — and is organized by the SAIR Foundation, building on Terence Tao's Equational Theories Project.

participation.howToSubmit: Submit a single solver.py (≤500 KB) via the official competition page; validate locally with scripts/run_harness.py and the pipeline runners.
participation.submissionFormat: One Python file solver.py implementing the track's I/O protocol (Solo: stdin/stdout JSON; Marathon: manifest-in/answers-out JSONL). If using the LLM in Solo, a module-level PROMPT string holds the template.
participation.computeDetails: ~12 GB disk (Lean toolchain + Mathlib olean cache), 8 GB RAM minimum / 16 GB recommended; LLM calls are proxied by the organizer.
participation.verification: Deterministic Lean judge (judge/verify.py) with five-status verdicts; same judge runs locally and at official evaluation.

competitions.quickstart:
bash scripts/setup.sh
pip install openai
source .env.judge
python3 scripts/run_harness.py
python3 -m pipeline.runner \
  --submission examples/solo/demos/baseline \
  --problems examples/problems/sample_20.json

competitions.name: Sutro Problems
competitions.tagline: Minimize the energy (read-cost) of small programs: matmul, sparse parity, symmetry, and MNIST on an A100.
competitions.description: A collection of small, self-contained problems used as benchmarks for the Sutro Group's energy-efficient learning research. Submissions are straight-line programs (IRs) or Python methods scored by a simplified Bill Dally data-movement model (reads cost ceil(sqrt(addr)), writes and arithmetic are free) or by wall-clock time and NVML energy on an A100. Records are merged into per-problem leaderboard tables via pull requests against main.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a pull request against main adding your .ir and generator under submissions/ and updating the accuracy band (table row) it improves.
participation.submissionFormat: A straight-line IR (plain text, v3 instruction set, <=2,000,000 lines) plus a Python generator and a markdown report; or for MNIST a Python method plus a standalone report under mnist/submissions/<name>/.
participation.computeDetails: MNIST-a100 tracks require an A100-80GB (official runs on Modal); matmul/sparse-parity/symmetry are scored symbolically with no GPU.
participation.verification: Symbolic verification (matmul.score_4x4/16x16, symmetry.score_six/eight), deterministic dev suite plus fresh random adjudication suite (sparse-parity), and sandboxed Modal A100 runs with NVML energy (mnist-a100).

cost = matmul.score_4x4(ir)

ir = mp.generate_scan(4095)
res = mp.evaluate_mask(ir)
res.cost, res.recovery

competitions.name: EmbedEval
competitions.tagline: Measures whether LLMs write safe embedded firmware C code from implicit domain knowledge, scored by pass@1.
competitions.description: EmbedEval is a benchmark of 267 embedded-firmware code-generation cases (219 public + 48 private held-out) across Zephyr RTOS, ESP-IDF, STM32 HAL, FreeRTOS, Linux kernel drivers and Yocto. Each case is scored through a 5-layer pipeline (L0 static, L1 compile, L2 runtime, L3 heuristic, L4 mutation) and the primary metric is pass@1 with Wilson 95% CIs. Prompts deliberately omit safety hints so the benchmark measures implicit embedded domain knowledge. Maintained by Ecro; results are published to a Hugging Face Space leaderboard.

participation.howToSubmit: Run `uv run embedeval run --model <litellm-id> --cases cases/` for n=3, then open a PR adding `results/runs/<date>_<model>/` and an updated `LEADERBOARD.md`.
participation.submissionFormat: Run archive directory (details/, summary.json, report.md) plus updated results/LEADERBOARD.md
participation.computeDetails: Default mode (L0+L3) needs no Docker; full L1/L2 build layers run in Docker images (embedeval-zephyr, Dockerfile.esp, Dockerfile.stm32). No GPU required.
participation.verification: Deterministic regex/pattern checks across 5 layers; scripts/verify_results.py re-runs checks on generated code; CI validates reference solutions.
requirements: Zephyr SDK / ESP-IDF / arm-none-eabi-gcc for full evaluation

competitions.quickstart:
git clone https://github.com/Ecro/embedeval.git
cd embedeval
uv sync
uv run embedeval run --model claude-code://sonnet --cases cases/
cat results/LEADERBOARD.md

competitions.name: SqueezeBench
competitions.tagline: Prove Lean-verified lower and upper bounds on extremal combinatorics functions to squeeze f between them.
competitions.description: SqueezeBench is a benchmark of Lean-verified bounds on extremal combinatorics problems such as Ramsey numbers, Schur numbers, cap sets and Golomb rulers. Each problem has a Lower and an Upper track; a submission is a Lean function ℕ → ℕ together with machine-checked proofs that it bounds f, is no worse than the current record, and is strictly better somewhere. Submissions are judged by Comparator against a frozen statement and checked by two independent kernels (Lean and nanoda), with no sorry, new axioms or native_decide. It is run by the SqueezeBench team (Pablo Manrique, Hai Xia, Stefan Szeider) and is designed as a saturation-resilient evaluation of mathematical capability.

participation.howToSubmit: Fork the repo, run `lake exe squeeze new <Problem> <lower|upper>` to lay out the next version, fill in Def.lean, Proof.lean, REPORT.md and metadata.toml, run `lake exe squeeze verify <record-dir> --base upstream/main`, then open a pull request that adds your record directory and nothing else.
participation.submissionFormat: One new record directory under SqueezeBench/Problems/<Problem>/Records/<Lower|Upper>/V<k>/ containing Def.lean, Proof.lean, REPORT.md and metadata.toml.
participation.computeDetails: Lean proof checking and Comparator verification run on CPU; the fuel check alone peaks near 7 GB of memory.
participation.verification: Comparator against a frozen statement, checked by Lean's kernel and nanoda (Rust re-implementation); no sorry, no new axioms, no native_decide.

organizer.name: SqueezeBench team (Pablo Manrique, Hai Xia, Stefan Szeider)

competitions.quickstart:
gh repo fork leansolving/SqueezeBench --clone
cd SqueezeBench
lake exe cache get
lake build
lake exe squeeze bootstrap
lake exe squeeze new <Problem> <lower|upper>
lake exe squeeze verify <record-dir> --base upstream/main

competitions.name: ProgramBench
competitions.tagline: Benchmark LLM coding agents on real-world software engineering tasks from GitHub issues.
competitions.description: ProgramBench evaluates AI coding agents on a suite of 200 software engineering tasks derived from real GitHub issues. Agents must produce patches that resolve the issues, and submissions are scored by the fraction of tasks resolved (mean score) and the fraction of instances attempted. The benchmark is run by Meta (facebookresearch) and the leaderboard is compiled from submissions in this registry repository.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a PR to this repository adding a folder `submissions/<submission_id>/` containing `pointer.yaml`, `submission.yaml`, and `_stats/` files. Use `programbench submit register <your-run-dir>` to automate the PR.
participation.submissionFormat: A folder with `pointer.yaml` (fork URL + pinned commit SHA), `submission.yaml` (manifest with model, provider, score headline), and `_stats/` containing `score.json` (required), `cost.json` (optional), `calls.json` (optional).
participation.computeDetails: Inference is run by the submitter; verification Tier-0 is CPU-only, Tier-1 re-runs eval which may require Docker.
participation.rounds: Continuous submissions; leaderboard recompiled on merge.
participation.eligibility: Open to anyone with a public submission fork.
participation.verification: Tier-0: recompute headline from `eval.json` and check against `submission.yaml`. Tier-1: re-run `programbench eval` on `submission.tar.gz` to confirm reproducibility.

competitions.quickstart:
git clone <a-public-submission-fork> && cd <fork>
uvx programbench submit verify .            # Tier-0: recompute headline vs manifest. No Docker.
uvx programbench submit verify . --tier1    # Tier-1: re-run eval and confirm the artifacts reproduce it.

problems.description: The main ProgramBench track: 200 software engineering tasks from GitHub issues, evaluated with the mini-SWE-agent harness. Score is the mean fraction of tasks resolved.

competitions.name: s2n-bignum-bench
competitions.tagline: Synthesize HOL Light tactic proofs for AWS s2n-bignum cryptographic theorems; scored by Pass@1 over a fixed problem set.
competitions.description: s2n-bignum-bench tests low-level code reasoning of LLMs by giving each problem a HOL Light goal from AWS s2n-bignum cryptographic proofs and asking for a HOL Light tactic chain that proves it. Answers are checked by compiling and running them in HOL Light, with per-problem verdicts of OK, FAIL, CHEATING, or ERROR, then aggregated into Pass@1 (and optionally Pass@K) scores. The corpus, scripts and evaluation harness are open source and maintained by the kings-crown project with contributors from AWS and academia, and results are submitted to an external leaderboard via GitHub issues.

participation.howToSubmit: Generate one answer per problem, evaluate locally to get results.csv, then zip your answers CSV and open a submission issue using the leaderboard repo's leaderboard-submission.yml template: https://github.com/kings-crown/s2n-bignum-leaderboard/issues/new?template=leaderboard-submission.yml
participation.submissionFormat: CSV with columns problem_id, category, query, answer (a HOL Light tactic chain proving each goal); answers may also be supplied as workdir/<problem-id>/answer.txt for local evaluation
participation.computeDetails: HOL Light proof checking is CPU-bound; each proof can use ~5 GB RAM, a safe rule is RAM_GB/6 parallel processes. A GPU with CUDA is needed only if you host a local LLM with vllm to attempt the problem set.
participation.rounds: Pass@1 (static combine-and-run) and Pass@K (checkpointed assessment) evaluation modes
participation.verification: HOL Light compiles and runs each submitted tactic; *.judge.txt files record OK, FAIL, CHEATING or ERROR, and collect-verdicts.py aggregates them into results.csv
requirements: Linux with bash, git, make, gcc
GPU + CUDA + vllm only if serving a local LLM to generate answers

competitions.quickstart:
git clone https://github.com/kings-crown/s2n-bignum-bench && cd s2n-bignum-bench
./setup.sh arm 4
python3 collect-problems.py toplevel-thms/ problems.json ml_files
python3 retrieve-problem.py retrieve --outputdir workdir --csv problems.csv --csv-only
# write workdir/<problem-id>/answer.txt for each problem
python3 combine-answer-and-setup.py workdir 8
./run-answers.sh eval-<timestamp> 8
python3 collect-verdicts.py eval-<timestamp> results.csv

problems.description: Given a HOL Light goal term extracted from the s2n-bignum proof corpus, produce a HOL Light tactic chain that proves it; scored by Pass@1 over the fixed problem set (with optional checkpointed Pass@K assessment).
problems.name: HOL Light Tactic Synthesis

competitions.name: Agent Anvil Public Leaderboard
competitions.tagline: Score agent tool-use safety with trace-aware assertions instead of final-answer-only checks.
competitions.description: Agent Anvil is a compact offline benchmark that compares final-answer-only grading with trace-aware assertions across tool-use safety scenarios. Authors run the benchmark in their own repo or CI, export a leaderboard_submission.json, and open a PR adding it under submissions/; CI validates provenance and rebuilds leaderboard.csv/json. Rows are ranked by trace-aware pass rate, with final-answer pass rate and answer-only missed failures reported alongside. Maintained by agent-axiom, with a live Hugging Face Space and Dataset.

participation.howToSubmit: Run Agent Anvil in your repo, export leaderboard_submission.json, copy it to submissions/<agent-name>.json, and open a PR to main; CI validates and rebuilds the index.
participation.submissionFormat: One JSON file per agent under submissions/ (schema agent-anvil.leaderboard.v1), generated by `anvil leaderboard export`; no raw traces, model outputs, secrets or PII.
participation.computeDetails: Compact offline benchmark (5 scenarios, 100 trials); runs locally or in GitHub Actions, no GPU required.
participation.eligibility: Open to any agent author with a public repository.
participation.verification: CI validates submissions, verifies github_actions run URLs via the GitHub API, checks GitHub artifact attestations, and runs `anvil leaderboard audit`; maintainer reruns are stored separately under maintainer_reruns/.

competitions.quickstart:
uv run anvil paper reproduce
uv run anvil leaderboard export docs/paper/results.json \
  --manifest experiments/paper.yaml \
  --out leaderboard_submission.json \
  --agent-name "My Agent" \
  --agent-version "2026-05-22" \
  --repo-url "https://github.com/acme/my-agent" \
  --commit-sha "$(git rev-parse HEAD)"
uv run anvil leaderboard validate leaderboard_submission.json

competitions.name: Modded-NanoGPT · Ascend NPU Leaderboard
competitions.tagline: Port and optimize NanoGPT speedrun records to run fastest on 8× Ascend 910C NPUs.
competitions.description: A fork of KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt that reproduces and optimizes upstream GPU speedrun records on eight Ascend 910C NPUs (16 dies). The task is to train a GPT-2-small-class model to ≤3.28 cross-entropy loss on the FineWeb validation set as fast as possible on the NPU hardware. Records are accepted with auditable source, launch commands, environment metadata, and successful run logs under records/track_1_short_npu/. The upstream GPU leaderboards are preserved for attribution.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a PR adding a record folder under records/track_1_short_npu/<record>/ with source/ and logs/ (successful .train.log files).
participation.submissionFormat: Source code snapshot, launch command, environment metadata, and successful training logs (.train.log) demonstrating ≤3.28 val loss.
participation.computeDetails: Eight Ascend 910C NPUs (16 dies, 16 distributed processes) using the reference Docker image docker.cnb.cool/nilpotenter/docker/codeserver-mindspeed:v1.0.5.
participation.verification: Human review of submitted source and logs; accepted records are benchmarked and reviewed before inclusion.

competitions.quickstart:
git clone https://github.com/zhaoyiyidan/modded-nanogpt-npu.git && cd modded-nanogpt-npu
# use the reference NPU image
docker run -it --rm -v $(pwd):/workspace docker.cnb.cool/nilpotenter/docker/codeserver-mindspeed:v1.0.5 bash
# inside container
/root/miniconda3/envs/llm_test/bin/python data/cached_fineweb10B.py 9
torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=16 train_gpt.py

competitions.name: Humanoid Parkour
competitions.tagline: Train an ONNX policy to walk a Unitree G1 through a 51 m parkour course; scored by course progress.
competitions.description: An Apex competition (Bittensor Subnet 1) where miners submit an ONNX policy (≤15 MB) that drives a 12-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid through a 51.1 m linear parkour course with ramps, drops, stairs, a 1 m leap, a hurdle, a step-up, a duck-under, a balance beam and a slick patch. Each round evaluates 24 instances of up to 3000 control steps with randomized, unobservable friction and wind drawn from a per-round seed. Scoring is progress-based: completions score in (1.0, 2.0] with a speed bonus, non-completions score their course fraction, and the mean over 24 instances is the raw score. The reference policy (Unitree's stock G1 walker) reaches only 21% of the course.

participation.howToSubmit: Submit an ONNX policy graph (≤15 MB) through the Apex platform; the referee runs it in a sandboxed player container against 24 randomized instances.
participation.submissionFormat: ONNX graph, ≤15 MB, float32, interface obs[104] + state_in[256] → action[12] + state_out[256]; architecture free (recurrent nets, ensembles, transformers over a history window).
participation.computeDetails: Referee runs under --cpus 1 --memory 1.5g; inference runs once per control step up to 72,000 times per evaluation. Training a policy typically needs GPU but evaluation is CPU-only.
participation.rounds: Rounds with per-round seeds for friction and wind; conditions not published while a round is open.

competitions.quickstart:
docker build -f referee/Dockerfile -t hp-referee .
docker build -f player/Dockerfile  -t hp-player  .
docker network create hpnet
docker run -d --name hp-p --network hpnet -v "$PWD/baseline/baseline.onnx:/app/submission.onnx:ro" hp-player
mkdir -p /tmp/hpdata && chmod 777 /tmp/hpdata
docker run --rm --network hpnet -v /tmp/hpdata:/data -e MATCH_ID=local -e SEED=1 -e NUM_PLAYERS=1 -e PLAYER_URLS=http://hp-p:8000 -e CONFIG_JSON='{"seed":1,"num_instances":24,"max_steps_per_episode":3000,"deadline_ms":500}' hp-referee
jq '.raw_scores, .metadata.num_completed' /tmp/hpdata/result.json

problems.description: Drive the 12-DoF Unitree G1 through the 51.1 m parkour course. Per-instance score: completions get 1.0 + (max_steps - steps)/max_steps in (1.0, 2.0]; falls/timeouts/out-of-bounds get the fraction of course covered in [0.0, 1.0); physics glitches/invalid/player errors get 0.0. raw_score is the mean over 24 instances.
problems.name: Humanoid Parkour Course

competitions.name: DepthDash
competitions.tagline: Find the fastest residual connection design to train a deep-narrow LM to a target loss on 8×H100.
competitions.description: DepthDash is a time-to-target speedrun built on the Modded-NanoGPT trainer, where the data, backbone, init and optimizer are frozen and a submission changes only the residual path (plus kernels and hyperparameters). Runs use one node of 8× NVIDIA H100 SXM and are scored by train_time to reach a target FineWeb validation cross-entropy loss at p < 0.01 over several seeds. Tracks 1 and 2 restrict changes to residual connections; Track 3 is open within a 5% parameter budget. It matters because DepthBench showed depth can be a scaling axis if residuals allow it.

participation.howToSubmit: Add records/<track>/<YYYY-MM-DD>_<Name>/ with the residual module (and fast model if used), logs of all seeds, check_equivalence.py output when a fast model is used, and a short README with time, mean val loss and p-value against the target.

participation.computeDetails: One node with 8× NVIDIA H100 SXM; compile warmup and validation are off the clock.
participation.verification: Logs must show at p < 0.01 that mean final val loss is at or below the track target; check_equivalence.py for fast models.

competitions.description: A modded-nanogpt-style speedrun benchmark: fix the task (40 canonical LAFAN1 clips on a Unitree G1), the hardware (1× Google Colab G4 / RTX PRO 6000) and the frozen referee, but leave the training algorithm, framework and simulator open. competitions.description: SiliconArena is an open research project toward manufacturable AI accelerator silicon, with training and inference tracks. competitions.name: StarVLA
competitions.tagline: A Lego-like open-source codebase for developing, training, and evaluating Vision-Language-Action models on robot benchmarks.
competitions.description: StarVLA is a modular research platform for building Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, with pluggable VLM backbones, interchangeable action heads (FAST, OFT, PI, GR00T), and benchmark-agnostic deployment hooks. It integrates a broad set of simulation and real-robot benchmarks (LIBERO, SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, RoboTwin, DOMINO, BEHAVIOR, CALVIN, RoboDojo, VLA-Arena, MetaWorld, Evo-DexBench) and reports SOTA results. The project is maintained by the StarVLA Community and released under the MIT License.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a PR to the repository following the contributing guidelines in docs/CONTRIBUTING.md; run Black + Ruff on changed files before submitting.
participation.submissionFormat: Code contributions (new framework variants, benchmark integrations, bug fixes) as pull requests; benchmark results documented in READMEs and model_zoo.md.
participation.computeDetails: Training typically uses multi-GPU setups (e.g., 8 processes with DeepSpeed ZeRO-2/3); can run on a single A100 with smaller VLMs like Florence-2.
participation.eligibility: Open to the community; MIT License permits commercial use, modification, and distribution.
participation.verification: Human review of pull requests; benchmark results reported by contributors.

competitions.name: Formal Conjectures
competitions.tagline: Formalise open mathematical conjectures as Lean 4 statements to build a benchmark for automated theorem provers.
competitions.description: Formal Conjectures is a Google DeepMind project collecting formalised statements of open mathematical conjectures in Lean 4 using mathlib. Contributors add or fix formalisations of conjectures from Erdős problems, Wikipedia, OEIS, arXiv papers and other sources; the repository is used as a benchmark for automated theorem provers and formalisation tools. Contributions are made via pull requests and reviewed by human maintainers, with periodic use of AlphaProof to detect misformalisations. Stable benchmark snapshots are tagged as bench-v{N}-lean4.{X}.{Y}.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a pull request to main adding or fixing a Lean 4 conjecture file under FormalConjectures/, following CONTRIBUTING.md conventions (file structure, @[category]/@[AMS]/@[question] attributes, style guidelines).
participation.submissionFormat: Lean 4 source files (.lean) containing formalised conjecture statements, with docstrings citing the original source URL; optional formal_proof links to external proofs.
participation.computeDetails: Lean 4 + mathlib build; `lake exe cache get` downloads prebuilt Mathlib oleans. No GPU required.
participation.eligibility: Open to all; contributors must sign the Google Contributor License Agreement.
participation.verification: Human review of pull requests by maintainers; CI runs `lake build` and `lake --wfail test`; periodic AlphaProof-assisted checks for misformalisations.

competitions.quickstart:
git clone https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures
cd formal-conjectures
lake exe cache get
lake build
lake --wfail test

competitions.name: SQuAD Leaderboard (Stanford Question Answering Dataset)
competitions.tagline: Maximize Exact Match and F1 on the SQuAD 1.1 and 2.0 reading-comprehension benchmarks.
competitions.description: SQuAD is a large reading-comprehension dataset of crowd-written questions over Wikipedia paragraphs, and this repository hosts the official explorer and leaderboard for it. Models are ranked by Exact Match (EM) and F1 on the held-out development set, with submissions made as prediction bundles through CodaLab Worksheets. The benchmark is maintained by the Stanford NLP group (Pranav Rajpurkar et al.) and remains a standard reference point for extractive question answering. SQuAD 2.0 additionally contains unanswerable questions, so models must decide when no answer is supported by the passage.

participation.howToSubmit: Upload model predictions on the official SQuAD dev set to CodaLab Worksheets as a bundle and register the bundle with the SQuAD leaderboard; each leaderboard entry links to its CodaLab bundle UUID.
participation.submissionFormat: Model predictions on the official development set, packaged as a CodaLab bundle; test-set scoring is done by the organizers against the withheld test set.
participation.verification: Official dev-set prediction bundles hosted on CodaLab necessitated a UUID per submission; test-set scores require evaluation by the organizers on the withheld test set.
requirements: SQuAD dev set predictions (SQuAD 1.1 or 2.0 format)

organizer.name: Stanford NLP Group (Pranav Rajpurkar et al.)

competitions.quickstart:
cl mimic 0x8f29fe78ffe545128caccab74eb06c57 <model_submission_uuid> <uuid_of_your_dataset>   # SQuAD 1.1
exit

competitions.name: Optimization Constants in Mathematics
competitions.tagline: Crowdsourced best known upper and lower bounds on optimization constants arising in mathematics.
competitions.description: A curated repository recording the best known upper and lower bounds on optimization constants C in mathematics, each arising from a variational problem or a best-constant functional inequality. Contributors submit improved bounds via pull requests, with certificates and checkers hosted externally; bounds are reviewed for plausibility and replicability but not certified for correctness. Maintained by Damek Davis, Paata Ivanisvili and Terence Tao.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a pull request to main adding or updating the constant page under constants/ and the corresponding README table row, with a reference and contribution note; supporting certificates/checkers are hosted externally.
participation.submissionFormat: Markdown edits to constants/<id>.md and README.md, plus a reference entry and contribution note; certificates, code and formalizations linked externally.
participation.computeDetails: Varies by constant; many bounds are computer-assisted with exact rational/interval arithmetic certificates, some use Lean 4 formalization.
participation.eligibility: Open to anyone; submissions reviewed for minimal plausibility and replicability.
participation.verification: Human review by maintainers; asterisk marks minimal verification; independent replays by a second party remove the asterisk; some bounds formalized in Lean 4.

organizer.name: Damek Davis, Paata Ivanisvili, Terence Tao

competitions.name: Terminal Bench 2.0 Leaderboard
competitions.tagline: Submit an agent that solves terminal-based coding and system tasks; ranked by task pass rate.
competitions.description: A community leaderboard for Terminal Bench 2.0, a benchmark of terminal-based coding and system administration tasks. Agents are run against the full task suite via a GitHub Actions scenario runner using Docker Compose, and scored by task pass rate (fraction of tasks solved). Submissions are made by forking the repo, configuring scenario.toml with an agentbeats.dev agent ID and an AGENT_LLM model string, and pushing to trigger the runner, which opens a results PR.

participation.howToSubmit: Fork the repository, fill in agent details in scenario.toml (agentbeats_id under [[participants]], AGENT_LLM model string, API keys as GitHub Secrets), then push to trigger the scenario runner; results are submitted as a pull request.
participation.submissionFormat: scenario.toml configuration plus GitHub Secrets for API keys; the workflow runs Terminal Bench 2.0 and merges shard results into one submission.
participation.computeDetails: Evaluation runs on GitHub Actions runners via Docker Compose; parallel evaluation is configured at the workflow layer (num_shards in .github/workflows/quick-submit.yml).
participation.eligibility: Open to anyone with a Terminal Bench 2.0-compatible agent and an agentbeats.dev ID.
participation.verification: Automated scenario runner (GitHub Actions workflow) executes Terminal Bench 2.0 against the submitted agent and submits results as a pull request.

problems.description: Agents are evaluated on the full Terminal Bench 2.0 task suite (terminal-based coding and system tasks) and ranked by task pass rate.
problems.name: Terminal Bench 2.0

competitions.name: GPU MODE Kernel Leaderboards
competitions.tagline: Write the fastest correct GPU kernel for a fixed operator; ranked by measured runtime on real NVIDIA and AMD hardware.
competitions.description: GPU MODE runs kernel-optimization competitions through KernelBot: each leaderboard fixes an operator (GEMM variants, attention decode, MoE, all-to-all, linear algebra, quantization, beginner primitives), a correctness checker, and a benchmark grid; submissions are timed on the organizers' GPUs and ranked by (geometric-mean) runtime. 42 leaderboards, 3197 ranked entries from 1619 users on B200, A100, B200_Nebius, MI355X, NVIDIA, MI300x8, H100, L4, MI300, T4; 8 currently accept submissions. Reference problems and evaluators live in gpu-mode/reference-kernels.

participation.howToSubmit: Pick a leaderboard, start from its starter submission.py in gpu-mode/reference-kernels, and submit through KernelBot: popcorn-cli (`popcorn submit submission.py --leaderboard <name>`), the GPU MODE Discord, or the editor on gpumode.com. Each submission is checked for correctness and timed on the leaderboard's GPUs.
participation.submissionFormat: A single Python file (submission.py) defining custom_kernel(data); CUDA, Triton or HIP code is embedded or loaded inline.
participation.computeDetails: Benchmarks run on GPU MODE's hardware (A100, H100, B200, L4, T4, MI300, MI300x8, MI355X); no local GPU is required, though one helps for iteration.
participation.deadline: per leaderboard; beginner v2 problems are open-ended
participation.prizes: varies by competition (sponsored rounds have prizes)
participation.eligibility: Open to everyone with an account.
participation.verification: Server-side correctness checks and timing; top submissions are re-validated against a stricter contract on some leaderboards.

competitions.quickstart:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gpu-mode/popcorn-cli/main/install.sh | bash
curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gpu-mode/reference-kernels/main/problems/linalg/cholesky_py/submission.py
# make custom_kernel faster, then:
popcorn submit submission.py --leaderboard cholesky --no-tui

competitions.name: P = NP?
competitions.tagline: An AI agent fleet works on P vs NP in Lean 4, live: your agent proves open steps the desk assigns, and only the proof checker decides.
competitions.description: pequalnp.com runs a coordinated fleet of AI agents against P vs NP in the open. Every step is a Lean 4 statement (on Mathlib and the project's own definitions) that counts only when the checker accepts a proof; refutations and dead ends stay on the record. The work runs on 6 fronts (Library of known results, Geometric complexity theory, Circuit lower bounds via algorithms, Proof complexity, Meta-complexity, P = NP algorithm search). Outside agents join by asking the desk for one open step and sending its proof as a pull request to open-goat/pequalnp-proofs. Since 2026-11-22: 17828 statements posted, 8400 checked, 5150 refuted; 825 outside contributors have had 7572 steps accepted. Tracks here: P vs NP itself and the open hard links each program is stuck on, then each front ranked by outside contributors' checked steps. The site records no model per step; attribution comes from the merged pull requests (commit trailers, "Generated with" lines, codex/ branches, the template's self-reported "Agent used").

participation.howToSubmit: Give your coding agent one line: "Fetch and follow the instructions at https://pequalnp.com/join.txt to work on P vs NP with me". It asks the desk for an open step (curl "https://pequalnp.com/desk/next?handle=<github handle>"), keeps the lease alive, writes one Lean file proving exactly the posted statement, and opens a pull request to open-goat/pequalnp-proofs (tools/pnp.sh next / check / submit does these steps). The checker posts ACCEPTED, REJECTED or FAULT on the pull request; an accepted proof is merged and credited to the GitHub handle.
participation.submissionFormat: One Lean 4 file per pull request, at the path the desk gives, proving the exact statement: no sorry, no new axiom, no native_decide, no # commands, macros or string literals, at most 512 KiB. A counterexample is sent as a proof of the step's negated twin; on steps open to reductions, a theorem deriving the step from 2 to 4 smaller statements is accepted too.
participation.computeDetails: Proving runs on your own machine with your own model usage; Lean with Mathlib needs about 10 GB of disk. The authoritative check runs on the project's runners: 20 minutes per file (more for outside imports, at most 45) and about 6.5 GB of memory.
participation.rounds: Continuous: the desk leases one open step at a time (up to five per handle); a lease lasts 20 minutes past its last renewal. Hard steps (&hard=1) are open problems the project is stuck on.
participation.prizes: Credit: accepted proofs are credited by GitHub handle on pequalnp.com and its public contributor leaderboard.
participation.eligibility: Anyone with a GitHub account.
participation.verification: Lean 4 checker on the project's runners: format rules are checked before the build, then the file must prove exactly the posted statement. Only the Lean file counts; nothing else in a pull request is read.
requirements: An AI coding agent that can run a shell, git and Lean (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, …)
GitHub account and the gh CLI signed in
About 10 GB of disk for Lean and Mathlib

competitions.quickstart:
# paste into your coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, …):
Fetch and follow the instructions at https://pequalnp.com/join.txt to work on P vs NP with me
# or by hand:
gh repo fork open-goat/pequalnp-proofs --clone && cd pequalnp-proofs
tools/pnp.sh setup
tools/pnp.sh next            # --hard for an open problem the project is stuck on
tools/pnp.sh check <step>
tools/pnp.sh submit <step>

problems.description: The question the whole project is for: a Lean proof, accepted by the checker, that P ≠ NP or that P = NP on the project's own definitions. pequalnp.com's verdict: open.
problems.name: P vs NP itself

problems.description: The hard link the Geometric complexity theory program is stuck on (L-gct-086, conjecture). A checked reduction [L-gct-077] turns a larger bound for the permanent into one statement: a linear bound on the dimension of linear spaces of matrices on which the permanent of the all-ones matrix plus a variable matrix stays constant. No proof route has survived yet, and today a complex space was found that real-number searches had missed, so the small-case evidence is being redone. The desk hands these out to agents that ask with &hard=1.
problems.name: Level spaces of the permanent at J are linear: dim L <= C n whenever perm(J_n + t) = n! on L

problems.description: The hard link the Circuit lower bounds via algorithms program is stuck on (L-clb-036, in work). No known method proves a circuit lower bound above linear size for an explicit problem in NP. The desk hands these out to agents that ask with &hard=1.
problems.name: SAT has no fan-in two circuits of size O(n^1.01)

problems.description: The hard link the Proof complexity program is stuck on (L-pcx-071, conjecture). About thirty attempts found true lemmas about how refutations of these formulas must look, and no way to count their lines; the printed method stops at a quadratic bound, and no short refutation was found either. The question is parked with its record. The desk hands these out to agents that ask with &hard=1.
problems.name: Dag-like Res(+) is not polynomially bounded on CNFs of constant width and constant F2 polynomial calculus degree

problems.description: The hard link the Meta-complexity program is stuck on (L-meta-3754, conjecture). Every counting argument tried on it failed where two such AND gates share a gate that other parts of the circuit read. Its first rung, exactly one such gate, is cut into twelve cases: two are checked, ten are conjectures waiting for proofs. The desk hands these out to agents that ask with &hard=1.
problems.name: Least lift-fixed circuits are clean: in a least lift-fixed fan-in-two AND/OR circuit for a 4-cycle-free bipartite edge function, every AND gate is below F

problems.description: Search for a polynomial time algorithm for an NP-complete problem. Any hit is held back under the security rule in ISOLATION.md. Aims at P = NP. Ranked by outside contributors' steps on this front that the Lean checker accepted; the fleet's own work is not ranked. The fleet's record here: 0 checked, 2 open conjectures, 3 refuted.
problems.name: P = NP algorithm search

competitions.name: First Proof
competitions.tagline: Unpublished research-level math problems; AI systems get one shot each and expert referees grade the proofs blind.
competitions.description: First Proof is an independent benchmark run by research mathematicians to measure whether AI systems can autonomously prove research-level results. Each batch collects problems that arose in the contributors' own work and whose proofs are unpublished; the editorial board runs every system itself, one shot per problem with no human input, and expert referees grade the proofs double blind. Batch 2 (2026-06-10): 4 systems, 39 graded solutions, 7 of 10 problems got at least one passing proof; P4, P8, P10 remain open. Batch 3 is under way; results are due 2026-10-14.

participation.howToSubmit: Systems enter per batch through the call for submissions on 1stproof.org. A system is an open-source harness calling publicly available models, or a public product; First Proof clones the submitter's repository, builds its Docker image on an approved EC2 instance and runs it once on the problem file, following the protocol published with each batch (e.g. 1stproof/batch-2).
participation.submissionFormat: A repository with Dockerfile, hardware.json, README.md and src/; the container reads the LaTeX problems from /data/input/input.json and writes LaTeX proofs to /data/output.
participation.computeDetails: Runs on First Proof's AWS instances; model API usage goes on the submitter's keys. Batch 2 systems spent $117–$4,799 in API fees for 10 problems.
participation.rounds: Batches of unpublished research problems, each graded and published with every solution and referee report, plus community experiments where problems are posted publicly and solutions follow a week later.
participation.eligibility: AI companies and academic teams; only publicly available models, or harnesses that will be released.
participation.cost: free to enter; API usage is paid by the submitter
participation.verification: Each proof is refereed double blind by at least two experts in the field; the editorial board decides essentially flawless, minor revisions, major revisions or reject. Problems, human solutions, AI solutions, referee reports and logs are all published.
requirements: Open-source harness or public AI product

competitions.name: Riemann Hypothesis Lean 4 Community Collaboration Hub
competitions.tagline: Shorten the pillars of the Lean 4 formalization that claims a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis: every run is machine-checked (0 sorry, standard axioms) and scored on normalized Lean tokens.
competitions.description: A community hub for the Lean 4 formalization that claims a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and of GRH for Dirichlet L-functions, announced by Levent Alpöge on 2026-11-20. The proof is split into pillars (sub-theorems with their own Lean entry point) plus the full proof as the Grand Challenge; entrants and their agents shorten a pillar's proof without breaking it. Bohrium's Agentic Science Playground builds and checks every submission (0 sorry, only the standard axioms) and scores it on its anti-golf normalized Lean token count; a run that beats the pillar's best score is kept as a breakthrough, and the hub's live board mirrors the results. 1,694 verified runs and 617 breakthroughs from 98 contributors (2,397 submissions in all) so far; 42 of 48 core pillars have a verified run, and their best proofs are 33.48% shorter in normalized tokens than the originals. Tracks here are the board's 49 pillars; each lists every author's best verified run, over a baseline row for the unmodified proof. Models and harnesses are what each author's CLI reported (self-reported telemetry); a row carries a model only where that text names one.

participation.howToSubmit: Scored on the board: install the Bohrium Playground CLI (curl -fsSL https://play.bohrium.com/install.sh | bash) and submit a shorter proof against any pillar's challenge on play.bohrium.com; it is built, checked and scored automatically, and frontier breakthroughs are staged in the hub as attributed draft pull requests. Directly on GitHub: fork Osgood001/riemann-hypothesis, simplify a module under src/, run scripts/pr_lightweight_checks.py and open a pull request against main; maintainers run the full Bohrium sandbox verification.
participation.submissionFormat: Lean 4 source for one pillar (a standalone file importing Mathlib, on the Lean version the pillar's Playground page names) that proves the pillar's statement with 0 sorry and only the standard axioms (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound).
participation.computeDetails: No GPU: proofs are built with Lean and Mathlib on your own machine and verified on Bohrium's sandbox, where the fast pillars check in minutes; building the full proof (the Grand Challenge) takes hours on a large machine and about 100 GB of disk.
participation.rounds: Pillars are added in phases (Core 1–5, Core 6–13, then the Phase 3 pillars); the Grand Challenge is the full proof.
participation.prizes: None stated; breakthroughs are credited on the board and staged in the hub as attributed draft pull requests.
participation.eligibility: Anyone; scoring on the board needs a Bohrium Playground account.
participation.verification: Every run is built and checked on Bohrium (0 sorry, standard axioms only, Lean Comparator) and scored on its normalized token count; a run that beats the pillar's best score is kept as a breakthrough. Models and harnesses on the board are self-reported telemetry.

competitions.quickstart:
curl -fsSL https://play.bohrium.com/install.sh | bash      # the Bohrium Playground CLI
# pick a pillar on https://riemann.verifytask.cn/: its Playground page has the statement and the original proof's size;
# shorten the proof, keep 0 sorry and only the standard axioms, and submit it against that challenge with the CLI
# or, for a pull request to the hub:
git clone --filter=blob:none https://github.com/Osgood001/riemann-hypothesis && cd riemann-hypothesis
python3 scripts/pr_lightweight_checks.py --base origin/main --head HEAD

competitions.name: The Looped Lens Challenge
competitions.tagline: Build an nnsight lens that reads what the looped model Inkling 2 Mini computes but never writes; NDIF runs it and a judge model scores it on hidden questions, ranked by pass rate.
competitions.description: NDIF's challenge for lenses on Inkling 2 Mini, a looped model: of its 24 layers, 6 to 17 run three times, so a token passes through 48 layer visits. A lens reads the model's internal state at up to 10 visits per question and returns up to 10 tokens per readout; a judge model checks which of five options (the intermediate the model works out but never writes, and four distractors) each layer names, and a question passes when the intermediate gets more layer votes than any other option. Lenses run on NDIF, which hosts the model, so entrants need no GPU; phases add harder questions, and the final ranking mixes early and later ones. Phase 1: 96 teams and 596 scored submissions so far (21 more under review); the organizers' reference lens (Starter logit lens) passes 66.19%. Tracks here are the leaderboard's phases; each lists every team's best submission not under review, over the organizers' reference lens. The leaderboard records no model or agent, so entries carry no attribution.

participation.howToSubmit: Get an NDIF API key (login.ndif.us) and register with the challenge's form using the same email (later registrations go on a waitlist; only admitted accounts can submit). Clone the repository, run uv sync, score submission/ on the practice questions with python submit.py --local, then submit with python submit.py --team "My Team" --wait (the team name the first time only); python submit.py --status lists your submissions. A team is one NDIF account and can submit once every 2 hours, with one submission queued or running at a time.
participation.submissionFormat: The submission/ directory (main.py, lenses.py, questions.py), at most 200 MB. The leaderboard runs main.py once per dataset; it writes $OUTPUT_DIR/readouts.jsonl with, per question, up to 10 readouts (one per layer visit, no layer twice) of up to 10 tokens each. Trained weights come from the Hugging Face Hub as safetensors, fetched at the top of the NDIF session.
participation.computeDetails: The lens runs on NDIF, which hosts Inkling 2 Mini, so no GPU is needed; a submission's run is limited to 45 minutes across all datasets.
participation.deadline: Phase 1 is open; its closing date is to be announced on the challenge page
participation.rounds: Phases: each phase is ranked on a new board; later phases add harder questions, and the final ranking mixes early and later questions.
participation.prizes: Prizes are mentioned in the challenge page's eligibility terms; amounts are not stated.
participation.eligibility: 18 or older; each person on one team; organizers and anyone who knows how the questions were built may not take part; US government-restricted or sanctioned parties are ineligible; only registered, admitted NDIF accounts can submit.
participation.verification: Every submission runs on NDIF and is scored by a judge model on hidden questions; winning submissions are audited, and one under review is flagged on the board while it keeps its place (left out here until cleared). The organizers may change the scored questions, the judge's prompts and the scoring code while the competition runs.
requirements: NDIF API key from an admitted account
Hugging Face account for trained weights (optional)

competitions.quickstart:
git clone https://github.com/ndif-team/looped-lens-challenge && cd looped-lens-challenge
uv sync && source .venv/bin/activate
export NDIF_API_KEY=...                   # from login.ndif.us; register with the challenge's form first
python submit.py --local                  # score submission/ on the practice questions
python submit.py --team "My Team" --wait  # submit; the team name is needed the first time only

problems.description: The current phase. A lens answers 290 hidden questions in 3 datasets (Dataset A, Dataset B, Dataset C); a question passes when the judge model finds the intermediate named on more of the lens's layer readouts than any of the four distractors, and a tie fails. Pass rate is the mean of the datasets' shares of questions passed, higher is better. 96 teams, 596 scored submissions; 21 submissions under review left out.

competitions.name: LeanEval
competitions.tagline: Prove open formalization problems in Lean 4; models and submitters are ranked by problems solved.
competitions.description: LeanEval is the Lean FRO's comparator-based benchmark for formal mathematics. Trusted theorem statements live in leanprover/lean-eval; a problem counts as solved when the comparator accepts a submitted proof. Results are sticky per (user, model, problem) and published at lean-lang.org/eval. 313 visible problems, 86 models, 67 submitters, 38 active problems still unsolved.

participation.howToSubmit: Prove a problem's theorem in your own GitHub repository and submit the ref at lean-lang.org/eval/submit; the comparator verifies the proof and the result is appended to results/<login>.json in leanprover/lean-eval-submissions.
participation.submissionFormat: GitHub repo + ref containing the completed Lean proof, plus the declared model label used to produce it.
participation.computeDetails: Scoring is a comparator check of the proof; whatever compute the prover needs is on the submitter's side.
participation.eligibility: Open to everyone. Successes are sticky: an accepted (user, model, problem) tuple is never removed.
participation.verification: Comparator acceptance in CI, replay by maintainers, public audit log per user.

competitions.quickstart:
git clone https://github.com/leanprover/lean-eval && cd lean-eval
lake exe cache get && lake build
lake exe lean-eval --help   # pick a problem under generated/, replace sorry, submit at lean-lang.org/eval/submit

competitions.name: Big O Speedrun
competitions.tagline: A race to improve the complexity bounds of classic problems (integer and matrix multiplication, 3SUM, APSP, 3-SAT, …); every record is Claimed, Human Verified or Lean Verified.
competitions.description: Big O Speedrun (bigospeedrun.com) tracks improved algorithmic bounds for classic problems; each race starts from the first result by AI agents that broke the classic bound. 10 races (Integer Multiplication, Matrix Multiplication, Fourier Transform, 3SUM, APSP, APSP, randomized, Subset Sum, 3-SAT, Integer Factoring, Directed Shortest Paths) and 20 "Other bounds" rows. Every result carries an evidence level: Claimed (published, not checked), Human Verified (accepted by the race's review repository) or Lean Verified (its Lean proof rebuilt and kernel-checked against the site's exact statement). New results are posted in #submit-a-result on Discord; Lean proofs go to bigospeedrun/verifier, and 4 races also take proofs from prove2.me campaigns. Tracks here list the current leader at each evidence level from the site's hourly data (updated 2026-11-26); a track ranks by the site's exact score where its page states one direction, otherwise by evidence level (each track says which). Agent attribution only where the site's text names the AI.

participation.howToSubmit: New results: Post a link to the public repository, commit or paper with the result in #submit-a-result on our Discord (https://discord.gg/JEN582WvNv). This applies to every problem, every Other bounds row and results that we missed. We list it as Claimed after we check that it states the same problem. Lean proofs (Fourier Transform, 3SUM, APSP, Subset Sum, 3-SAT, Directed Shortest Paths): Submit the Lean proof to bigospeedrun/verifier as a pull request or an issue. It shows as Lean Verified when it passes. The verifier checks a proof only if its bound matches or beats the best Lean Verified result on that board; a Claimed result does not block it. It is the main path for these problems (instructions: https://github.com/bigospeedrun/verifier#submit). prove2.me (Integer Multiplication, Matrix Multiplication, 3SUM, APSP): An additional way for the problems listed here: prove the bound on prove2.me, which checks each proof with Lean on its server, in the campaign of the race. When a proof states our exact problem, we review it, and it shows as Lean Verified, with a link to prove2.me, after our next hourly refresh. Review repositories: If a problem lists a repository with acceptsSubmissions true, also open a pull request there. Its maintainer reviews it. A pull request is Claimed while it is open, or when it was merged only for archival intake: the repository's review ledger (docs…
participation.submissionFormat: A link to a public repository, commit or paper that states the bound for the race's exact problem; for Lean Verified, a Lean 4 proof of the verifier's statement (pull request or issue on bigospeedrun/verifier, or a proof in the race's prove2.me campaign).
participation.computeDetails: Research and Lean proof building run on your own machine with your own model usage; the site rebuilds a Lean proof from source and checks it with the Lean kernel (Comparator) against its exact statement.
participation.rounds: Continuous: the site's data is refreshed hourly; a race closes when a result is shown to be the best possible.
participation.prizes: Recognition: records are listed on bigospeedrun.com and announced on X and Discord.
participation.eligibility: Anyone.
participation.verification: Claimed: The result is published, but no review repository accepted it and we have not checked a Lean proof. Human Verified: The result meets the repository review rule stated on the problem page. Lean Verified: We rebuild its Lean proof from source and check, with the Lean kernel, that it proves our exact problem statement. A result also counts when prove2.me, which checks each proof with Lean on its server, proved it and we reviewed that its Lean statement is our problem statement. A result also counts when at least two people other than its authors each publish their own build of its Lean proof and a…
