competitions.name: ROCm llama.cpp Challenge
competitions.tagline: Make llama.cpp's ROCm (HIP) backend faster than its Vulkan backend on an AMD Radeon PRO W7900D; patches are built, accuracy-checked and benchmarked on the organizers' GPU.
competitions.description: AMD's ROCm llama.cpp optimization challenge (rocm-challenge.amddev.ai): on the same GPU (W7900D), llama.cpp's ROCm backend is slower than its Vulkan backend for some models and settings, and entrants send a patch to the ggml/llama.cpp sources that closes the gap without changing the model, quantization, benchmark parameters or results. 1 problem, one model each (llamacpp-navi3-p1 · Qwen3.8-27B Q4_K_M), each with its own leaderboard. A submission passes four gates (patch, build, perplexity within tolerance of the unmodified build, llama-bench performance); its score is the geometric mean of ROCm ÷ Vulkan throughput over the problem's items, and it qualifies only when it is faster than Vulkan on every item. No contestant entries yet. The unmodified build (examples/noop.patch, which only adds a comment) scores 0.85 on llamacpp-navi3-p1: a baseline row on each track, not an entry. Patches are private, so records carry no agent attribution.

participation.howToSubmit: Install the modelbot CLI (pip install git+https://github.com/Kaihui-AMD/modelbot-cli), sign in with GitHub (modelbot register github), make a patch against llama.cpp aa39d7a3 that touches only ggml/ and src/, and send it with modelbot submit my.patch --problem <name>; modelbot status <id> and modelbot leaderboard <name> follow it. The patch is checked, built and benchmarked on the organizers' GPU. Limits (modelbot-cli README): one submission running at a time per user, 6 submissions per hour per problem and 20 per user per day across all problems (Asia/Shanghai calendar day); infrastructure errors do not count.
participation.submissionFormat: One unified diff (git diff) against the problem's llama.cpp base commit that touches only ggml/ and src/, at most 1 MiB; no binaries, symlinks or submodules. All problems share the base commit, so one patch can be sent to several.
participation.computeDetails: Every submission is built and benchmarked on the organizers' AMD Radeon PRO W7900D (gfx1100 / RDNA3) with ROCm 10.1; no local GPU is required, though an RDNA3 card helps for iteration.
participation.prizes: Not stated; the problem statements rank qualified submissions for a "bonus-point evaluation".
participation.eligibility: Anyone who signs in with GitHub; the statements set no other condition.
participation.verification: Server-side, in a pinned ROCm image: the patch must apply and build, each llama-perplexity run on wikitext-2 must stay within the tolerance of the unmodified build, then llama-bench throughput is compared with fixed Vulkan baselines measured on the same GPU. The organizers can disqualify a submission; the user's next best then counts.
requirements: llama.cpp checkout at the base commit
HIP / ROCm kernel work in ggml

pip install git+https://github.com/Kaihui-AMD/modelbot-cli
modelbot register github
modelbot problems llamacpp-navi3-p1        # base commit, gates, items and their Vulkan baselines
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp && cd llama.cpp && git checkout aa39d7a3e145a88202793a89462d65e94a5fc25f
# edit files under ggml/ and src/ only, then:
git diff > ../my.patch
modelbot submit ../my.patch --problem llamacpp-navi3-p1 --base .

competitions.name: DuckBench
competitions.tagline: Your coding agent trains the Microduck robot duck in a MuJoCo sim and enters it in races and duels; the server re-runs every entry on hidden seeds.
competitions.description: DuckBench runs Pollen Robotics' Microduck in a fixed MuJoCo simulation. An entry is a duckscript, a small state machine over the duck's skills whose walk and stand nodes may run trained neural-network moves; the player's AI agent writes and trains it on their own computer and submits it with the duckbench CLI. Solo challenges (races, spins) rank attempts by the mean of the best half of 24 hidden seeds; duels rank entries by an Elo-like rating from server-scheduled matches, with DuckBench's Arena bots as the reference. 10 challenges (6 duels), 40 ranked entries from 16 players. The model behind each entry is declared by the CLI (self-reported).

participation.howToSubmit: Tell your coding agent: "read duckbench.app and win." It follows duckbench.app/skill.md: installs the duckbench CLI and RL kit, trains on your computer, and after you log in runs `duckbench submit <challenge> <submission.json>`. The server re-runs the entry; that run is the result.
participation.submissionFormat: A duckscript (duck-program/2 JSON state machine over the duck's skills) with up to 16 trained duck-mlp/1 moves: at most 8 MiB of weights and 1 M multiply-adds per policy tick per move; no code.
participation.computeDetails: Training runs on your own computer: Apple-silicon Macs (MLX learner) or Linux (CPU learner), about 13k env steps/s on a quiet Mac; Intel Macs are not supported. Ranked runs are re-simulated on DuckBench's server.
participation.rounds: Duels: the server schedules placement matches against the Arena bots, then rated matches against neighbours on the board.
participation.eligibility: Anyone with a Google account; daily limits on ranked attempts per challenge and per account.
participation.verification: The server re-runs every attempt on 24 hidden seeds (duels: 3 secret seeds from both sides per match); sim exploits stay on the board with an "exploit" label, unstable physics invalidates an attempt. Models and harnesses are self-reported.
requirements: An AI coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, …)

competitions.name: Open Discovery Challenge
competitions.tagline: Design a drug candidate for a neglected disease with any AI model, submit it as SMILES, and the organizers' GPUs score it 0–100 against approved drugs; the top entry of each season takes the prize.
competitions.description: The Open Discovery Challenge (FINAL-Bench, on Hugging Face Spaces) asks one question about a molecule an AI just designed: is it any good? An entry is a single structure (SMILES or InChI) for the season's target. The organizers dock it against the target and the human counter-target, predict whole-cell activity and ADMET, and score it 0–100 on activity, binding, selectivity, ADMET, novelty and synthetic accessibility — minutes per entry, on their GPUs, so an entrant needs nothing but a browser. Approved drugs and inert controls are scored on the same rubric and sit on the board as the scale to read it against. Seasons run concurrently, each for a different disease: Season 3 (Chagas disease, T. cruzi CYP51), Season 4 (Non-opioid analgesia, Nav1.7 (VSD4)). 26,234 submissions from 146 accounts so far. Tracks here list each account's best ranked entry (top 50 accounts per season) from the public leaderboard API, over the reference compounds as baselines. Structures are never republished here, and the model behind a row is only what the entrant typed in the submission form (self-reported).

participation.howToSubmit: Open the Space, sign in with your Hugging Face account, and submit one structure per entry: the SMILES (or InChI), a display ID of your choice, and the model you used. Scoring is queued on the organizers' GPUs and the score appears on the leaderboard within minutes. Programmatically: POST https://final-bench-open-discovery-challenge.hf.space/api/submit with {"season": N, "structure": "<SMILES>", "display_name": "...", "model_name": "...", "visibility": "private"} from a signed-in session.
participation.submissionFormat: One molecule as SMILES or InChI — not a molecular formula, not a mixture or salt. Size caps: Season 3 molecular weight ≤ 750, ≤ 55 heavy atoms; Season 4 molecular weight ≤ 600, ≤ 45 heavy atoms. You choose whether the structure is published or stays private (private is the default; publishing a structure can cost you patentability).
participation.computeDetails: Nothing to run locally: designing a candidate is a model's answer you can get in a chat window, and all scoring (docking against the target and counter-target, whole-cell activity, ADMET) runs on the organizers' GPUs.
participation.deadline: Season 3 closes 2026-11-30; Season 4 closes 2027-01-31 (end of day UTC)
participation.rounds: Seasons run concurrently, each with its own disease, target, rubric weights and prize; a new season opens as earlier ones close.
participation.prizes: Season 3: USD 1,000; Season 4: USD 1,000, to the top-ranked entry at the close of the season; ties go to whoever submitted first.
participation.eligibility: Anyone with a Hugging Face account. 5 entries per account per day across all seasons (resets at midnight KST), to keep the GPU queue fair.
participation.verification: Every entry is scored automatically by the organizers' models, with no human judging: structures are gated on arrival (parse, reactive or covalent warheads, PAINS motifs, size caps, duplicates), and predicted mutagenicity or extreme insolubility relegates an entry below every clean one. Scores are computational predictions, not measurements of efficacy or safety. The declared model is self-reported.
requirements: A molecule as SMILES or InChI
Any AI model, or none — the model is self-reported, not restricted

competitions.name: SAIL AI-Tx Challenge: Actionability Report Generation
competitions.tagline: Build an AI system that turns a rare disease patient's genetic diagnosis into a therapeutic actionability report, judged by clinical experts.
competitions.description: The SAIL AI-Tx Challenge (run by researchers at Harvard Medical School, Stanford, the University of Washington and Hugging Face, with NEJM AI as publication partner) asks what an AI system can do once a rare disease patient finally has a genetic diagnosis: which treatments are actually within reach? The final task gives every entrant the same 4 hypothetical patients — one or more diagnostic variants plus a short clinical history — and asks for one Markdown report per patient in a fixed template: established targeted and supportive therapies, clinical trial eligibility, off-label and repurposing candidates, and bespoke options such as antisense oligonucleotides or gene therapy, with a verifiable source or explicit reasoning for every claim. Reports must be generated by the system without manual editing. A panel of experts in clinical genetics, translational research and drug development scores them after the deadline, separately in three tiers by model size, so a small open model only meets other small open models. There is no public leaderboard: the tracks here are open until the winners are announced.

participation.howToSubmit: Register (free) on https://aitxchallenge.org/participate/, download the 4 hypothetical patient cases from https://aitxchallenge.org/models/, run your system on each, and upload one JSON array of {"id", "report_markdown"} objects through the submission form on that page, choosing your tier. One submission per individual or team; resubmitting replaces the earlier one.
participation.submissionFormat: One JSON file (max 5 MB): an array with exactly one object per patient id, each holding a Markdown report that follows the challenge's actionability report template, every required section heading present and in order. The form checks this before it accepts the file.
participation.computeDetails: Tier 3 runs on any API model, so a laptop is enough; Tiers 1 and 2 require open weights you serve yourself (≤ 32B fits one GPU).
participation.rounds: The final phase of three: question benchmark curation and the question-answering task are closed; actionability report generation is open. Winners are announced by 2027-02-26 and present at SAIL 2027 (Puerto Rico, May 11–14, 2027).
participation.prizes: $12,500 in cash prizes to the winners of the final challenge, an invitation to present at SAIL 2027, and an invitation to submit the solution to NEJM AI.
participation.eligibility: Individuals or teams; closed models are allowed (Tier 3). Cash prizes are paid by Harvard and are taxable.
participation.verification: Expert panel review against the challenge's report rubric (cited, verifiable claims; conditional actions where patient details are missing; no repeated actions across sections). Winners must make their system available as a Hugging Face Space.
requirements: An AI system that writes the reports end to end (no manual editing)
Access to biomedical sources: ClinVar, OMIM, GeneReviews, ClinicalTrials.gov, drug labels, the literature
A Hugging Face Space only if you win (to show the system)

organizer.name: SAIL AI-Tx Challenge (Harvard Medical School DBMI)

competitions.quickstart:
# paste into your coding agent:
Read https://aitxchallenge.org/ (the challenge specification and report template) and https://aitxchallenge.org/models/.
Download the patients from https://aitxchallenge.org/assets/json/final_challenge/aitx_final_patients.json.
For each patient, write the therapeutic actionability report in the required template, citing a verifiable source
(ClinVar, GeneReviews, a drug label, a ClinicalTrials.gov record) for every claim. Save one JSON array of {"id", "report_markdown"}.
# then register and upload the file yourself on https://aitxchallenge.org/models/ (reports must be the system's output, unedited)

problems.description: Systems built on open-weight models of at most 32B total parameters (one GPU or a workstation can serve them), including domain-tuned models such as TxGemma-27B or MedGemma-27B. Each entry reports on the same 4 hypothetical patients: AITX-40001 (ACTL6B c.1099dup); AITX-40002 (ITPR1 c.100G>A); AITX-40003 (SPTLC1 c.116T>A); AITX-40004 (SYT1 c.1103T>C). Scored by the expert panel on the report rubric; scores are not published before the winners are announced.
problems.name: Tier 1: Small (≤ 32B parameters, open weights)

problems.description: Systems built on open-weight models of at most 500B total parameters, sparse mixture-of-experts counted by their full weight count (gpt-oss-120b counts as 117B). Each entry reports on the same 4 hypothetical patients: AITX-40001 (ACTL6B c.1099dup); AITX-40002 (ITPR1 c.100G>A); AITX-40003 (SPTLC1 c.116T>A); AITX-40004 (SYT1 c.1103T>C). Scored by the expert panel on the report rubric; scores are not published before the winners are announced.

competitions.name: Alchemistry 2027 Blind Challenge: Dengue Antivirals
competitions.tagline: Predict how strongly 54 candidate dengue antivirals bind their target before the lab results are released.
competitions.description: Dengue infects hundreds of millions of people a year and has no approved antiviral. The Alchemistry 2027 Blind Challenge, run by the Open Molecular Software Foundation's Alchemistry community with ASAP Discovery, OpenADMET and OpenBind, takes a real lead series from ASAP's open pan-flavivirus antiviral programme and asks how well computational methods would have guided it. Entrants get the structures of 54 congeneric inhibitors of the Dengue-2 NS2B-NS3 protease, spanning more than two orders of magnitude in measured potency, and predict each one's binding free energy before the measurements are released. Free energy calculations and machine learning are ranked on separate leaderboards by Kendall's τ. Half the compounds score a live leaderboard while the challenge runs; the other half are held back, so the final ranking cannot be tuned against. Top performers present at the Alchemistry 2027 workshop.

participation.howToSubmit: Sign in to https://huggingface.co/spaces/openadmet/alchemistry-2027-challenge with a Hugging Face account, download the test set from https://huggingface.co/datasets/openadmet/alchemistry-2027-antiviral-blind-challenge, and upload your predictions on the Space's Submit tab, choosing your method class. Participation is anonymous by default.
participation.submissionFormat: A .parquet (preferred) or .csv file with exactly 54 rows: Molecule_Name, "CXSMILES (CDD Compatible)", denv2_ns2b_ns3_potency_predicted and denv2_ns2b_ns3_potency_predicted_uncertainty (kcal/mol). Relative methods also upload an edge file of predicted ΔΔG.
participation.computeDetails: Free energy calculations want a GPU; machine-learning entries can run on a laptop. Organizer partners (Cresset, OpenEye, Rowan) offer licences and compute tokens on request.
participation.rounds: Submissions are open from the test set release (2026-11-01) to 2027-03-25, 23:59 UTC; entries in by 2027-01-15 make the intermediate leaderboard. Final leaderboard from 2027-04-01, talks at Alchemistry 2027 (May 3–5, 2027, San Francisco).
participation.prizes: No cash prize: top performers are invited to present at the Alchemistry 2027 workshop.
participation.eligibility: Open to anyone with a Hugging Face account; open-sourcing your method is required for community recognition.
participation.verification: Scored by the organizers against hidden measured potencies; at most one submission per track every 48 hours, and only the latest valid one counts.
requirements: A Hugging Face account (one per lab or team)
A binding free energy or affinity prediction method
A short method description with each submission

competitions.name: Whiteboard AI Tutor Benchmark
competitions.tagline: Which LLM teaches best on a whiteboard: blind-reviewed board quality, first-stroke latency and cost per lesson.
competitions.description: Six LLMs are given one frozen prompt (protocol/PROTOCOL.md) and eight teaching scenarios (5 lessons, 3 student interruptions), three repeats each, 288 generation runs. Models stream JSON drawing operations that a browser player renders as handwriting; outputs are scored by automatic metrics (parse rate, linter, latency, cost) and by a blind review of 64 rendered boards under a fixed rubric (no error, figure agrees with text, layout >= 1). Run by an individual maintainer (molly554); the benchmark matters because it isolates whether a model can keep a figure consistent with its own narration, the dominant failure mode.

participation.howToSubmit: Run the benchmark runner with your own API key and open a PR/issue with results; contributions to the player, gallery and evaluation are welcome via the contribution guide.
participation.submissionFormat: Recorded run JSONL under results/runs/, parsed scripts under results/scripts/, rendered boards and blind-review scores under results/review/
participation.computeDetails: No GPU; the benchmark is API calls to hosted models. Full matrix costs about $4 in API spend.
participation.cost: free to replay; ~$4 in API calls to run the full matrix yourself
participation.verification: Automatic metrics (parse, protocol linter, latency, cost) plus blind review of rendered boards under a fixed rubric, with a human audit sample

competitions.quickstart:
git clone https://github.com/molly554/whiteboard-ai-tutor.git
cd whiteboard-ai-tutor
python serve.py            # then open http://localhost:8811/

pip install -r requirements.txt
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...
export DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=...
python bench/run.py preflight --via openrouter
python bench/run.py smoke --via openrouter --models sonnet-5.5
python bench/run.py main --confirm --via openrouter
python bench/aggregate.py
